title: Turkish, Kazakh, and Malaysian Companies Hit With New US Sanctions Over Iran
gist: New US Treasury sanctions under 'Operation Economic Outcast' hit 36 entities in Turkiye, Kazakhstan and Malaysia to ground Iranian airlines, while Hormuz commodity transits have collapsed to roughly six to twelve vessels a day against a 2025 pre-strike average of more than 100 — undercutting US claims of controlling the strait.

insights.claim: On September 8 the US Treasury announced sanctions on 36 entities, including cargo service providers and general sales agents based in Turkiye, Kazakhstan and Malaysia, aimed at grounding Iranian airlines as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.'
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Sanctions exposure is extending to logistics intermediaries in Central Asia and Southeast Asia — a compliance risk vector for regional aviation and freight firms.
insights.locator: the U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions

insights.claim: The targeting of general sales agents and cargo service providers rather than Iranian carriers themselves shows the enforcement mechanism now runs through the commercial service layer that makes airline operations possible.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Expect further designations of servicing intermediaries rather than principals; screen counterparty exposure at the agent level.
insights.locator: The sanctions hit 36 entities, including cargo service providers

insights.claim: Six commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on September 8, down from nine the previous day and below the 10-day average of about 12, according to Reuters.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Daily Hormuz transit counts are the highest-frequency read on Gulf supply disruption; these levels imply severe ongoing constraint on seaborne energy flows.
insights.quote: six ​commodity vessels passed through the strait on September 8, “down from ‌nine a day earlier and below the 10-day average of about 12.”

insights.claim: In 2025, before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, more than 100 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day on average, meaning current traffic is running at roughly a tenth of the pre-conflict baseline.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: An order-of-magnitude collapse in Hormuz transits is a structural supply shock for crude, LNG and refined products; the pre-strike 100+ baseline is the recovery benchmark to watch.
insights.quote: In 2025, before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, more than 100 commodity vessels passed through the strait each day on average.
insights.locator: In 2025, before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran

insights.claim: Although the US government claims to be in control of the vital Strait of Hormuz, traffic remains low, indicating that military control of the waterway has not translated into restored commercial flows.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Do not treat declarations of strait control as a signal to unwind shipping or energy risk premia — commercial willingness to transit is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: Although the U.S. government claims to be in control of the vital Strait of Hormuz, traffic remains low.

insights.claim: The Trump administration's war against Iran has stretched into its seventh month, making this a sustained conflict rather than a short punitive campaign.
insights.speaker: Catherine Putz
insights.so_what: Seven months of conflict with no restoration of Hormuz traffic argues for pricing in persistence rather than near-term normalization.
insights.locator: The Trump administration’s war against Iran has stretched into its seventh month
